title: EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards celebrates a decade of excellence
article:
The EdgeProp Singapore Excellence Awards (EPEA) marks its 10-year milestone in 2026, recognising outstanding property developments for their design, innovation, landscape, sustainability and sales performance.

Established in 2017, the awards set out to create a credible benchmark for Singapore’s leading property developers and developments. Over the past decade, EPEA has attracted more than 550 submissions, with 67 developments and 14 developers receiving top accolades.

What excellence means for homebuyers

For homebuyers, the awards provide another reference point when evaluating a property purchase. Beyond location and price, the design and execution of a development can influence the way residents experience their homes.

Thoughtful layouts, well-planned communal spaces and cohesive landscaping can make a difference to everyday living, while integrated sustainability features contribute to a development’s long-term efficiency and appeal.

This year’s EPEA theme, “ Celebrating a Decade of Excellence ”, reflects the awards’ focus on developments that go beyond function and aesthetics.

The emphasis is on creating homes and communal spaces that enhance residents’ quality of life, comfort and convenience, with design and innovation delivering tangible benefits.

A live-work-play environment

In addition to residential properties, the awards recognise offices, industrial developments, retail spaces, hotels and co-living projects, reflecting the diverse roles real estate plays in daily life.

Together, these sectors can create a vibrant live-work-play environment, encompassing places to live and stay, workplaces and destinations for shopping, dining, socialising and recreation.

Excellence takes different forms across property sectors, depending on how spaces are planned, designed, used and experienced.

In residential developments, for instance, this may mean enhancing liveability and the functionality of shared spaces, while offices and retail developments respond to the needs of their occupiers and visitors.

Across these sectors, design, functionality and sustainability contribute to a development’s overall quality, relevance and long-term value.

Recognising developments beyond Singapore

For the first time, the awards will also celebrate exemplary developments in Malaysia and Australia. The introduction of these accolades reflects the interest among Singaporeans in property markets beyond their home country, whether for investment or their own use.

For buyers considering an overseas property, the winning projects offer a useful starting point for exploring the market, understanding what different developments offer and conducting further due diligence. Differences in ownership rules, financing, taxation and ongoing costs remain important considerations, alongside the location and characteristics of each development.

Ten years on, EPEA continues to spotlight developments distinguished by considered design, innovation, landscape and sustainability. These qualities can help homebuyers assess how well a property meets their needs, while offering investors a fuller picture of its appeal and long-term potential.

title: Google debt-risk gauge rises as earnings revive AI debt jitters
article:
(Oct 29): The cost of insuring against losses on Alphabet Inc’s debt rose on Thursday as its shares plummeted, after disappointing results intensified fears that its massive bet on debt-funded artificial intelligence (AI) spending may fail to pay off.

The price of five-year credit default swaps on Google’s debt, which increases as investor concern grows, rose as much as 5.3 basis points (bps) to 84bps a year, according to ICE Data Services. It’s the biggest increase since Sept 21. Costs also rose for the likes of fellow hyperscaler Meta Platforms Inc and chip company Broadcom Inc.

The Google and YouTube parent reported weaker-than-expected revenue for the third quarter. That includes ad sales, a critical for financing Alphabet’s massive AI investments and which posted its lowest growth in more than a year.

While equity investors could see huge gains if AI investments pay off, debtholders bear the pain if things unravel, according to Gavan Nolan, fixed-income-pricing executive director at S&P Global Market Intelligence. Bond investors are laser-focused on capital spending and when AI revenue will be free cash flow positive, he added.

“In some way credit is telling a bit of a different story than equities when it comes to the tech sector,” Nolan said in an interview.

Trading volume for CDS tied to the 10 largest hyperscalers and chipmakers surged more than eightfold this year to US$176 billion through last week, according to an analysis of trade repository data by Barclays plc credit strategist Jigar Patel. Some of the swaps, like for SpaceX, have only started trading in recent months.

See also: Asia leads US-friendly nations in cutting their purchases of Treasury by 60%

Most active are Oracle Corp swaps, Patel said, with 2026 volume rising by nearly six times from last year’s level to US$46.8 billion.

title: Lagarde downplays inflation risk as ECB holds, announces her early exit
article:
(Oct 29): European Central Bank (ECB) president Christine Lagarde played down the danger that inflation will spread beyond energy after news that she will step down early overshadowed Thursday’s decision to leave interest rates untouched.

Lagarde tried to keep her press conference focused on monetary policy, revealing that she and her colleagues discussed and rejected the idea of a hike. Behind that move is a lack of evidence that surging energy prices are triggering things like excessive wage demands and significantly higher inflation expectations.

But with investors leaning towards another quarter-point increase in the deposit rate in December, she left space for further tightening, calling the direction of travel for the ECB “clear”.

“We are very attentive, and at this point in time, we are not seeing risk of second-round effects in addition to what is already included in the projections,” Lagarde told reporters on Thursday in Frankfurt. “We do not see material risk of second-round effects at the moment.”

Market wagers on a rate hike at December’s meeting edged higher, reaching 22 basis points, equivalent to an 88% chance compared with 80% before Thursday’s decision. The euro trimmed a small drop to remain little-changed versus the dollar at US$1.1153.

See also: Race to replace Lagarde begins after she announces leaving ECB in early 2027

Lagarde’s premature departure, on Feb 7, added to concern over energy costs and France. The moves ignited a race between the former central-bank chiefs of Spain and the Netherlands to succeed her in overseeing policy for the eurozone.

On borrowing costs, the ECB is biding its time having hiked twice since the Iran war jolted energy markets. It joins the US Federal Reserve in holding rates steady this week, with the Bank of Japan expected to follow suit on Friday.

Policymakers in Frankfurt are widely expected to raise again in December, when they will get updated economic projections. Rising global bond yields — exacerbated by the market, budgetary and political tensions gripping France — are damping demand.

See also: Bank of Canada raises rates to 2.5%, says more could be needed

“While the full effects of the energy shock are still unfolding, underlying inflation has remained broadly stable so far and wages do not show a material response at this stage,” the ECB said in a statement. “Financing conditions have tightened since the Governing Council’s last meeting, which is likely to weigh on inflation and growth.”

Lagarde, too, zeroed in on gains in core prices, which exclude volatile items like energy and food. “Underlying inflation will probably take a particular standing in the three-prong approach that we apply to our monetary-policy decision,” she said.

The latest rally in energy helped drive the headline gauge of consumer prices up 3.8% in September, with inflation expectations also creeping higher. Oil has jumped by more than 6% since the ECB last set rates, while natural gas hit its highest level in almost four years.

The economy may be starting to feel the pinch: Business momentum and morale are faltering. Third-quarter growth probably slowed to 0.2%, according to a Bloomberg poll of analysts before Eurostat publishes data on Friday. Rate increases contributed to a fall in demand for loans during that period.

“The incoming data suggests that the euro-area economy continued to expand in the third quarter,” Lagarde said, describing risks to the outlook as to the downside. “At the same time, renewed energy-price increases have hit consumer confidence, and higher financing costs are likely to weigh.”

title: Race to replace Lagarde begins after she announces leaving ECB in early 2027
article:
(Oct 29): President Christine Lagarde announced she will leave the European Central Bank (ECB) in early 2027, intensifying the struggle to replace one of the world’s most powerful monetary policymakers.

Lagarde will step down on Feb 7, according to an ECB statement on Thursday. She became the institution’s fourth leader, and the second from France, when she replaced Mario Draghi in 2019. Her term was due to end in October 2027.

“I leave this institution with a sense of good work done, and an ECB that is fit for the future,” Lagarde said in a video message. She is departing to be able to better engage in matters like events in France, according to people familiar with what she told the Governing Council on Thursday.

German bonds and their euro-area peers held small gains. The yield on 10-year German debt remained one basis point lower at 3.36%, while the premium on French bonds held steady at 154 basis points.

Lagarde’s departure sets up one of Europe’s most consequential leadership contests, with the winner to oversee interest rates for the eurozone’s 21 member states and their more than 350 million people.

“To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today (Thursday) and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision by the European Council,” European Council president Antonio Costa said in a statement.

See also: Bank of Canada raises rates to 2.5%, says more could be needed

The Eurogroup will act swiftly to prepare the recommendation for the next ECB president, its head Kyriakos Pierrakakis said in a statement. A decision will be reached by the end of the year, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said.

The move comes at a delicate time for the Frankfurt-based ECB, which is battling elevated inflation caused by the Iran war, against a backdrop of volatile geopolitics, nervy bond markets and massive European spending on defence and infrastructure.

Spain’s Pablo Hernandez de Cos and the Netherlands’ Klaas Knot are vying for Lagarde’s job. Economists surveyed by Bloomberg in October reckon De Cos, a former Bank of Spain chief who currently heads the Bank for International Settlements, is the favourite.

See also: French consumer confidence drops to 13-year low following riots

Talk about Lagarde’s exit had been building. She had repeatedly declined to commit to finishing her eight-year term. Speculation has been rife, meanwhile, that she wants to take over the World Economic Forum, the organiser of the annual Davos gathering.

Lagarde has also indicated she may like to play a role in campaigning for French presidential elections next spring, but ruled out running for the top job. The cryptic remarks have frustrated colleagues at the ECB, with some worrying it’s a bad look for one of the region’s most important economic institutions.

“Throughout its history, the ECB has successfully managed leadership transitions while continuing to fulfil its mandate,” Lagarde said in a memo to staff. “This situation is no different. I know that the ECB will continue to serve Europe with the same dedication during the period ahead.”

The announcement arrives with the US and Iran still failing to strike a lasting peace deal. The ECB lifted borrowing costs in June and September, and markets expect policy to be tightened further.

Bond yields, meanwhile, have spiked around the globe, with investors becoming particularly nervous about public finances in Lagarde’s home country of France. The premium they demand to hold the nation’s 10-year bonds compared with those of Germany recently hit its highest since 2011, leading to speculation of possible ECB intervention.

While Lagarde has argued that projections point to inflation returning towards target around the end of 2027, critics will accuse her of breaking promises to not abandon her post when “there are clouds on the horizon”.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Before Lagarde, the Netherlands’ Wim Duisenberg was the only president to not complete a full term. But his curtailed stint was agreed in advance to resolve a deadlock between France and Germany before the ECB’s inception in 1998.

European leaders have summits in November and December where they try to select a successor. Beyond the front runners, an outsider can’t be excluded, with Lagarde herself having only entered the frame at the last minute.

Governments must also select a successor for Isabel Schnabel, who’s cutting her term short by a year and will leave in early 2027 to join the the International Monetary Fund. With chief economist Philip Lane’s mandate also up in May, they will probably seek to strike a deal on all three positions.

Lagarde’s premature departure risks drawing accusations of political encroachment on the ECB’s independence, as the timeline now allows President Emmanuel Macron to help replace her before his final terms ends. Polls suggest far-right candidate Marine Le Pen could win the first round of elections for the Elysee.

France’s central-bank chief also resigned early, with Macron appointing Emmanuel Moulin, his chief of staff, to the position.

title: Anthropic IPO may spark AI rally as short bets on tech pile up
article:
(Oct 29): Wall Street’s recent risk aversion towards stocks may have created an opening for a sharp rebound, particularly in technology shares, if Anthropic PBC’s planned initial public offering reignites enthusiasm for artificial intelligence.

Investors have reduced their equities exposure to levels broadly in line with historical norms, according to Deutsche Bank. Discretionary investors have cut their exposure to US equities to the lowest in more than a month, while funds that use computer-driven trading strategies have also scaled back. That leaves room for renewed buying if confidence returns.

Hedge funds have gone further, increasingly betting that stocks will fall. Goldman Sachs Group Inc says its hedge fund clients have sold short roughly US$5 worth of stocks for every US$1 in purchases this month. Hedge funds’ use of borrowed money to bet against stocks is now near its highest level in five years, according to the firm’s records.

Those bets could help fuel a rally if stocks take off, forcing investors who wagered on declines to buy shares to close out their positions.

Technology stocks have been hit especially hard, seeing their heaviest two weeks of net selling in more than a decade of Goldman records through Oct 16. Deutsche Bank says investors have sharply reduced their technology holdings since early October, bringing them to a six-month low near levels seen during the Iran war.

The Nasdaq 100 Index has fallen 4.5% since Oct 6 as investor sentiment deteriorated amid a challenging macro backdrop. Brent crude climbed as the war in Iran continued, fuelling worries over higher inflation and elevated interest rates. At the same time, concerns about the sustainability of the AI investment boom have intensified. Comments from cloud-computing provider CoreWeave highlighted the risks of financing AI infrastructure with debt, particularly as interest rates rise.

See also: Mi Material closes at $1.82 on first day of trading; Stabilisation manager bought 1.5 mil shares at IPO price of $1.80

That retreat could make technology shares particularly sensitive to a change in sentiment. A successful Anthropic IPO could renew excitement about AI and encourage investors to return to the sector.

“Investors have been repositioning portfolios as tech and semi leadership has been challenged and we have approached levels where investors just need reassurance that the AI story is still on track,” said Joe Gilbert, portfolio manager at Integrity Asset Management. “The Anthropic IPO will be a critical test for markets once we get past earnings. Similar to the SpaceX IPO, investors will be looking for exposure to a unicorn stock that is one of one — at least until OpenAI comes public — and we believe the demand will be strong.”

Individual investors could also help drive a rebound. From late August to early October, retail investors were buying options betting on stock gains at an unusually high rate compared with those betting on declines. That activity has slowed over the past two weeks, although it remains above average, suggesting investors may have more appetite for buying.

See also: Metasurface to raise $9.82 mil via IPO placement of 18 mil new shares at 54 cents each

“We believe this shows more room for retail investors to add to the AI trade,” John Marshall, a partner at investment firm Carrick Lane, wrote.

SpaceX’s stock market debut offers an example of how a major IPO can attract individual investors. On Friday, June 12, the day the company went public, those investors bought more US stocks than they sold by the largest amount recorded in a single day on Citadel Securities’ platform. The firm handles about 35% of US-listed stock trading by individual investors. Trading in both stocks and options surged.

“There was astronomically large retail participation,” said Scott Rubner, head of equity and equity derivatives strategy at Citadel Securities.

Still, not all investors have been pulling back and dry powder my be running short at long-only funds. Barclays data show that while hedge funds have reduced their bets on rising stock prices, traditional investment funds have continued buying US equities.

Investors have poured about US$340 billion into US stock funds this year, more than three times the roughly US$100 billion typically invested by this point, according to Barclays’ Stefano Pascale. Funds that actively pick stocks now hold less than 1% of their assets in cash, suggesting they have already invested much of the money available to them.

That could limit how much additional buying comes from those investors, even if enthusiasm for AI returns.
